t: Introduction: physical factors and body temperature
n: This topic is devoted to the effects of physical factors and body temperature. Under normal conditions, body temperature is 36–37 °C. When the temperature is below 22–25 °C or above 43–44 °C, changes incompatible with life occur in the tissues. The general effect of high temperature leads to heat stroke, and its local effect to thermal burns. The general effect of low temperature causes general hypothermia, and its local effect causes frostbite.

t: Heat loss and conditions for heat stroke
n: Heat loss and conditions for heat stroke. Excess heat is shed 55 % by radiation, 27 % by sweat, 15 % by conduction and 3 % by various excretions. Heat stroke occurs when a lot of heat is produced and little is lost: with high air temperature and humidity, no wind, in a hot workshop and during heavy physical work. Clothing that does not let air and moisture through, cardiovascular disease, obesity and old age predispose to it. Children under one year of age are extremely sensitive to heat stroke.

Mechanism of heat stroke. The leading role is played by haemodynamic disturbance: the blood thickens and circulation slows. This intensifies tissue hyperthermia, that is, the hyperthermia increases, and leads to tissue hypoxia. At the same time, catecholamines and glucocorticoids are released in the stress reaction. Stasis and disturbed permeability are observed in the microcirculation.

t: Forms and periods of heat stroke
n: Forms and periods of heat stroke. The acute form occurs in an unacclimatised organism: consciousness is suddenly lost, coma begins and death follows within a short time. The protracted form has three periods: the first is depression of CNS function, the second is excitation, and the third is prostration. In the period of prostration, that is, the preagonal period, the temperature may exceed 41–42 °C. When it rises above 42–43 °C, death occurs from primary respiratory arrest.

Sunstroke occurs from prolonged exposure of the head to the sun's rays when it is uncovered. Signs: headache, clouding of consciousness, hallucinations and convulsions. A marked rise in body temperature is not typical. Signs of a first-degree burn, that is, erythema, may be present on the skin. In death from heat stroke and sunstroke, the changes are similar and non-specific: cerebral congestion and oedema, and petechial haemorrhages. Rigor develops quickly, whereas the lividity appears late and is scanty.

t: Thermal burns: causes, first and second degree
n: Thermal burns: causes, first and second degree. A thermal burn forms when the temperature in the skin and subcutaneous tissue exceeds 45–50 °C; in areas of thin skin it is deeper. Causes: flame, boiling viscous substances, that is, tar, napalm and bitumen, water hotter than 60 °C, steam, gases and a heated object. First degree shows as erythema and resolves without a trace in 3–4 days. Second degree presents with blisters containing serous fluid and heals without scarring in 10–20 days.

Third- and fourth-degree burns. Third degree is characterised by necrosis with exudative inflammation. In III-A, the epidermis and the superficial layer of the dermis undergo necrosis, whereas in III-B the necrosis is complete. Fourth degree involves necrosis of the skin and deep tissues, that is, muscle, ligaments and bone; granulation forms in the second to third week, followed by a scar. First- and second-degree burns are considered superficial, and third- and fourth-degree burns deep. Remember: fourth degree occurs only from the action of flame.

t: Determining the source of a burn
n: Determining the source of a burn. With hot liquid, hair and clothing are not damaged; the burn is superficial, in the form of streaks. Flame damages hair and clothing, the wounds are tongue-shaped and deep, and traces of soot are found. A heated object leaves a deep, circumscribed burn. A burn of the airways is characteristic only of steam and hot gases. These signs help to determine the source of the burn.

Determining the burn area. The area is determined by the rule of nines; this rule was proposed by A. Wallace in 1951. According to it, the head and neck account for 9 %, an arm 9 %, the front of the trunk 18 %, and the back of the trunk 18 %. A thigh is 9 %, the lower leg and foot 9 %, and the perineum 1 %. In the palm rule, the palm is taken as approximately 1 %.

t: Burn severity and recording the diagnosis
n: Burn severity and recording the diagnosis. The following are considered life-threatening: a third- to fourth-degree burn of more than 10 % of the surface, a third-degree burn of more than 15 %, and a second-degree burn of more than 20 %. A burn accompanied by oedema of the airways and narrowing of the glottis is also life-threatening. In the diagnosis, the burn is written as a fraction: the area in the numerator and the degree in the denominator, for example 10 % / II.

Burn disease. Burn disease develops if a first-degree burn covers more than 50 % of the surface, or a second- to fourth-degree burn covers more than 10–15 %. Its periods follow one another: burn shock, toxaemia, septicotoxaemia and convalescence. Burn shock lasts up to one day, sometimes 2–3 days. Toxaemia lasts 1–2 weeks, and septicotoxaemia from 2–3 weeks to several months. In young children the disease is more severe than in adults, even when the area and depth are not large.

t: Vitality of the action of flame
n: Vitality of the action of flame. In bodies recovered from fires, death most often results from carbon monoxide poisoning, and the body is charred afterwards. If soot is present in the airways, oesophagus and stomach, this shows that the flame acted during life. Carboxyhaemoglobin is also an important indicator: with postmortem exposure it does not exceed 20 %, while with exposure during life it may reach 60 %.

t: Other signs of vitality and the burnt body
n: Other signs of vitality and the burnt body. The following indicate vitality: the "crow's foot" sign, that is, absence of burning at the bottom of the eyelid folds, burns of the airways, an arterial thrombus and pulmonary fat embolism. In blisters formed during life, the protein content is twice that of postmortem blisters. Epidural haematomas are also distinguished: a traumatic haematoma is spindle-shaped, while a postmortem one is crescent-shaped and not attached to the dura mater. A burnt body may show the "pugilistic attitude".

t: Low temperature: factors and general effect
n: Low temperature: factors and general effect. High humidity, wind, clothing unsuited to the season, fatigue, hunger and alcohol intoxication intensify the effect of low temperature. Children and the elderly are considered susceptible. In almost all cases, the effect of low temperature is the result of an accident. In cold water the time to death is short, 1–1.5 hours; on sudden immersion, death may occur from vascular collapse or cold shock.

Stages of general hypothermia. First comes the compensation stage: metabolism increases, glycogen decreases and the skin vessels constrict. In decompensation, when the temperature falls to +30…+28 °C, cortical function is disturbed; each 1 °C fall slows the processes roughly twofold. The final stage is at +25…+22 °C: death most often results from primary respiratory arrest, and sometimes from collapse or ventricular fibrillation.

External signs of general hypothermia. In the "frozen person's posture", the arms are flexed to the chest and the legs to the abdomen; in severe intoxication this may be absent. The exposed areas are bluish and swollen. Icicles are found around the mouth and nose, and hoar frost on the eyebrows and eyelashes; these are the signs of M. I. Rayskiy. "Goose skin" is also observed. In men the testicles are contracted and the scrotum drawn up toward the inguinal canal; this is the sign of K. V. Puparev.

Cadaveric lividity and internal signs. Because the blood is rich in oxygen, the lividity is pinkish-red; at above-zero temperatures, up to +10 °C, it may be bluish-violet. The internal organs are congested, and the left chambers of the heart and the aorta contain bright scarlet blood. The stomach is empty and small; this is the sign of V. I. Pukhnarevich. Small haemorrhages are present in the mucosa of the renal pelves; this is the sign of P. A. Fabrikantov. The urinary bladder is full of urine.

Vishnevskiy spots. Small haemorrhages are found in the mucosa of the stomach, and sometimes the duodenum; these are S. M. Vishnevskiy spots. They occur in 80–90 % of deaths from hypothermia and may be detected even 6–9 months after death; their diameter is up to 0.5 cm. When death occurs quickly, the spots are very few or absent. For this reason they are often not seen in young children.

Microscopic and histochemical changes. Under the microscope one sees microcirculatory spasm, stromal oedema and petechial haemorrhages, and bronchospasm; there are also changes in the straight tubules of the kidney, which is Kasyanov's sign. On histochemistry, glycogen disappears from the liver, pancreas, heart and brain, and lipoids from the adrenal cortex. In severe intoxication, the blood alcohol concentration may be low and the urine concentration high.

The frozen body. At sub-zero temperatures a body may freeze regardless of the cause of death; therefore injuries produced by freezing must be distinguished from those inflicted during life. On freezing, the volume of the brain and parenchymatous organs increases. In the cranial cavity, bone fractures and separation of the sutures are possible. The body is thawed at room temperature; rapid thawing, up to +50 °C, increases haemolysis and imbibition.

Frostbite. Here the general temperature is normal, while in a particular area it is lowered. The fingertips and toes, ear, nose and cheek are most often affected; there are latent and reactive periods. First degree shows as reddish-bluish colour and swelling lasting 3–7 days. In second degree, clear blisters form, lasting 10–20 days. In third degree, necrosis occurs and a scar forms in 1–2 months. In fourth degree, necrosis down to the bone and purulent complications are seen. In the reperfusion phenomenon, changes may also develop in the opposite arm or leg. Life-threatening is frostbite of more than 10 % in third to fourth degree, more than 15 % in third degree, and more than 20 % in second degree.

General information on electrical injury. It accounts for 1–2.5 % of all injuries, but holds one of the leading places for disability and death. In most cases it is caused by technical current and, by circumstances, is an accident; lightning strike is very rare. The peculiarity is that current cannot be detected without a special instrument. Even though the exposure is brief, there is a disproportion between the magnitude and the severity of the consequences.

Properties of electric current. In industry and daily life, alternating current is mainly used; up to 500 V alternating current is more dangerous, and above 500 V direct current. The international standard for safe voltage is 24 V. Most deaths occur at 220–380 V; above 3000 V, an electric arc produces a local burn. A current of 50 mA threatens life, and at 100 mA most outcomes are fatal. A frequency of 40–60 Hz is extremely dangerous, while a frequency above 10000 Hz does not cause injury.

t: Factors related to the body and the environment
n: Factors related to the body and the environment. Children, the elderly and pregnant women are more susceptible. Cardiovascular disease, intoxication, trauma and heat stroke lower resistance. The order of increasing resistance is: blood, mucosa, liver, kidney, muscle, brain, lung, ligament, cartilage, nerve, bone, skin. Moist skin and sweating increase the effect; for this reason fatal electrical injury is more common in summer, that is, it is seasonal.

t: Conditions of exposure: duration, contact, current loop
n: Conditions of exposure: duration, contact and current loop. At 10–15 mA, involuntary muscle contraction occurs. At a current above 25 mA, spasm of the respiratory muscles is observed. At 80 mA and above, ventricular fibrillation develops. With two-pole contact, or single-pole contact with earthing, the current spreads; single-pole contact of a body insulated from the ground is usually safe. The "current loops" passing through the heart and brain, that is, the upper, left, left oblique and full left loops, are life-threatening.

Step voltage and electric arc. Step voltage is the difference in potential between two points on the ground separated by the length of a stride, 0.8 m. One should not approach a broken conductor closer than 10 m. High-voltage current can cause injury without touch, through an electric arc; at very high voltage the arc length reaches 35 cm. When humidity is high, the conductivity of the air rises and the risk of injury increases.

t: General and chemical-thermal effects of current
n: General and chemical-thermal effects of current. The general effect produces ventricular fibrillation, respiratory disturbance, shock and vascular injury. Electrogenic asphyxia is related to a direct effect on the respiratory centre, clonic convulsions of the respiratory muscles and spasm of the glottis. In the chemical effect, coagulative necrosis forms on the anode side and colliquative necrosis on the cathode side. In the thermal effect, "pearl beads" 1–5 mm in diameter appear in the bone.

The electric mark forms at the points where current enters and leaves; the local temperature reaches 120 °C, and it is more evident in areas with a thick horny layer. It is round or oval and firm, with raised edges and a depressed centre; the surrounding skin is unchanged and the hair is not singed. Metallisation gives colour: copper gives blue, green, yellowish-brown; iron yellow, brown, black; aluminium grey, yellowish-brown; lead grey, dusky. Methods of detection: colour prints, the radiological method and emission spectrography.

t: Electrical burns and types of death
n: An electrical burn forms at high voltage, when the local temperature exceeds 120 °C. It is painless, and no inflammation is seen around it. The true width and depth become evident after 2–3 weeks and are several times greater than at first. Types of death according to M. I. Avdeev: ultra-rapid, slow, interrupted and late. Because of apparent death, that is, vita minima, resuscitation is recommended until cadaveric lividity appears.

Lightning, that is, atmospheric electric current, is a discharge with a voltage of millions of volts, a strength of hundreds of thousands of amperes and a duration of ten-thousandths of a second. The damaging factors are electric current, light, sound and the shock wave. Burns may be present on clothing, and metal objects may melt. The red or pink tree-like "lightning figure" on the skin is considered the specific sign. It disappears after several hours, sometimes after a day, so it is photographed immediately.

Barotrauma and high pressure. Barotrauma is rare in forensic practice; it is observed in diving, flying, explosions, high mountains and pressure chambers. When pressure rises slowly to 6 MPa, there are no serious morphological changes. A sharp rise, however, leads to barotrauma of the lungs, ears and nasal cavities. Hydrostatic pressure at a depth of 10 m is 2 times atmospheric, and at 20 m, 3 times.

Barotrauma of the lungs. With scuba use, in 80 % of cases pulmonary barotrauma is the cause of death, and in 20 % drowning. On ascent from a depth of 10 m, holding the breath sharply raises the intrapulmonary pressure and leads to barotrauma. The bronchi and alveoli rupture, and emphysema and pneumothorax develop. In the acute period, death most often occurs from air embolism of the cerebral arteries.

Ear, nose and body squeeze. In ear barotrauma, the tympanic membrane ruptures and the middle and inner ear are injured. Haemorrhage is seen in the nasal cavities, but it does not lead to death. Body squeeze is specific to divers: it results from damage to the diving suit, hose failure or being inverted head down. Signs: the head enlarges, the face turns blue and swells, many petechial haemorrhages appear, and there are symmetrical haemorrhages corresponding to the edge of the helmet.

t: Effects of oxygen, carbon dioxide and nitrogen
n: Effects of oxygen, carbon dioxide and nitrogen. In oxygen poisoning, the neurotoxic form is seen at pressures above 2.5–3.0 MPa, and the pulmonary form at 1.0–1.5 MPa with exposure of more than 2 hours. Children are more resistant to oxygen, so the acute form does not occur in them. Carbon dioxide is poisonous at 3 % and above. Nitrogen dissolves in fat 5 times better than in blood and produces a state resembling intoxication.

Decompression, or caisson, disease. First stage: on rapid ascent, nitrogen dissolved in the blood and tissues forms bubbles of free gas. Second stage: they obstruct the blood vessels. Third stage, localisation: bubbles are found in blood and lymphatic vessels, joint cavities, bile and cerebrospinal fluid. Fourth stage, in the body: gas clots in the right chambers of the heart and veins, and subcutaneous emphysema. Fifth stage: a frothy fluid is found on the cut surface of the liver.

Low pressure and altitude sickness. At low pressure, the partial pressure of oxygen falls, and decompression disturbances and "boiling" of fluids are seen. Altitude sickness occurs in non-acclimatised people at an altitude of 3500–4000 m. At 5000–7000 m, uncompensated hypoxia develops. At 6000–8000 m, decompression signs appear. At 18000 m, that is, at a pressure of 6 kPa, 45 mm Hg, tissue fluids "boil".

Pressure factors of an explosion. In explosions of great force, high and low pressure act together: a zone of very high pressure is followed by a zone of extremely low pressure. As a result, various injuries characteristic of both states may be inflicted. In a direct lightning strike, severe injuries such as traumatic amputation of limbs arise, as in blast trauma.

t: Radiation: types and effect on the cell
n: Radiation: types and effect on the cell. Radiation injury is seen in nuclear explosions, reactor accidents, scientific work and medicine, that is, radiodiagnosis and radiotherapy; apart from an explosion, it is regarded as an accident. Neutrons, gamma rays and X-rays are highly penetrating. Alpha and beta particles have low penetration, and most are stopped by clothing. Ionising radiation suppresses cell division; this is especially marked in bone marrow, lymphoid follicles, skin, the gastrointestinal tract and the gonads.

Radiation sickness: forms and dose. At a dose up to 10 Gy the bone marrow form develops, at 10–20 Gy the intestinal form, at 20–80 Gy the toxaemic form, and above 80 Gy the cerebral form. The bone marrow form leads to death at a dose above 6 Gy. In acute radiation sickness, when the dose exceeds 1–2 Gy, the primary reaction lasts up to 3–4 days, the latent period 2–4 weeks, and then the overt clinical period begins. With a single dose of 50 Gy, death occurs in the first two days, and with a dose over 150 Gy, immediately, from paralysis of the brain centres.

t: Death from radiation and the expert's tasks
n: Death from radiation and the expert's tasks. In the overt period, death occurs against a background of multiple haemorrhages in the skin and organs, destructive changes in the bone marrow, lymph nodes and spleen, and infectious complications. Necrotic gingivitis, loosening and loss of teeth are found in the mouth. The expert's tasks: to determine the type of damaging factor, the nature of the source, the dose, the number and time of exposures, and the severity of bodily harm.
